comments.text:
It depends if you consider yourself artist and/or if you consider yourself as a designer.

If you regard yourself as an artist, I still strongly think generative AI does not produce art. Using a base sketch helps, but the rendering afterwards is not art.

As a designer, where it’s more umbrella, and the priority is the result, not the journey, you still have an issue where the generated image will have errors in it. If you had made the whole thing by hand, those mistakes would simply be your human fingerprint. If it’s machine-generated mistakes, it now becomes “insufficient quality control if you don’t fix them post-generation.”

Interestingly, the user needs to pay to generate the image. It’s money going to Adobe and not another artist whose style options you’d think would work well, and would use that money as income.

One risk with using generated images as moodboard/references/inspiration is that it has been shown that generative AI compounds biases. As you say, you need to ensure you’re in control of the creative process. Which I would ask, wouldn’t you have to be less alert if you didn’t use generative AI? The only motivation I can see for using it in workflow is: curiosity or a tight deadline. Creative deadlines are often pressured by our Capitalist society, who care about efficiency and economic value only.

In a vacuum, the video is quite interesting, and the tool looks fun to experiment with. But we’re not in a vacuum. And there’s still a lot of work that needs to be done in legal systems to ensure no one is getting exploited by this Pandora’s Box.

comments.text:
I agree with your approach overall, but I think there’s an important twist. Even when you use AI to help you find better questions, you still have to be the one steering that process. You can’t just say ‘give me better questions’ and expect something meaningful. That’s cutting yourself out of the creative process.

A better approach is to start with your own questions and ask AI to critique them. Where are they vague? What assumptions are baked in? What’s missing? That way you’re guiding the refinement instead of outsourcing it.

The same thing applies creatively. If I ask AI to write lyrics, I’ll get something generic. But if I write something myself and ask what’s not working, the feedback can be very useful. It’s not very good at writing lyrics, but AI is great at pointing out obvious weaknesses that you might miss.

And this is where people go wrong: don’t say ‘find better words’ or ‘fix the meter.’ That’s a bad habit. You’re handing over the creative decisions. Instead, ask ‘what’s wrong with this?’ Then you do the work of fixing it.

AI is at its best when it sharpens your thinking, not when it replaces it. Even the questions about your questions need to be directed by you, or you’re just drifting.
